title: Spot the invisible change
summary: One flipped bit. A completely different fingerprint.
body:
A cryptographic hash turns a file into a fixed-size fingerprint. SHA-256 produces 256 bits, shown as 64 hexadecimal characters.

Change one bit in the file and its hash will almost certainly change. Compare against a trusted hash of the original to detect damage.

A matching hash is useful evidence of integrity, but a checksum alone does not prove who created a file. A hash also cannot restore missing or damaged data. You need an intact copy for that.

title: Bring the signal back
summary: Detect the damage. Then recover from an intact copy.
body:
A checksum can tell you a file changed. It cannot reconstruct the original. An intact backup can.

In this challenge, save a copy, damage the working message, then restore the saved bytes. The matching SHA-256 fingerprints confirm recovery.

This tab-memory demonstration is not a real backup: closing or reloading the tab clears it. Real backups need independent storage and tested restores. The 3-2-1 approach keeps three copies on two kinds of media, with one copy off-site. Bitrot's freeze command does not create a backup; local files never decay automatically.
